children: Hindalco is integrating resource efficiency into its manufacturing and governance systems, with a focus on waste utilisation, water conservation, emissions reduction and biodiversity

Hindalco Industries is shifting its sustainability approach from managing environmental impact to making resource efficiency part of how the business operates, according to Vaishali Surawar, Chief Sustainability Officer, Hindalco Industries.

Speaking at the 9th Sustainable World Conclave, Surawar said the company’s scale of operations makes efficient resource use a business responsibility. Hindalco operates across 10 countries, with 48 manufacturing plants, 24 mines and 15,000 hectares of operating area under management. Its operations include the production of aluminium, copper and alumina.
“Primary metals are inherently resource intensive,” Surawar said, adding that the larger the industrial footprint, the greater the opportunity to create a positive impact.
Waste Moves From Liability To Input
One of the biggest areas of focus for Hindalco is industrial waste. Surawar said the company is looking at waste not simply as a disposal issue, but as a potential raw material for other industries.

Hindalco generates 14.42 million metric tonnes of waste annually, of which 88 per cent is utilised. The company recycled 12.64 million metric tonnes of waste, while 2.05 million metric tonnes of legacy waste was utilised last year, according to the company’s presentation.

The materials are being used across applications including cement, road construction, bricks and other construction materials. Nine Hindalco factories have also received Zero Waste to Landfill certification, which includes verification of how waste is handled after it leaves the company’s facilities.
The company is also working on older waste sites, including rehabilitation and the evacuation of legacy waste for productive applications.
Water Efficiency Becomes A Business Metric
Water is another area where Hindalco is attempting to reduce its dependence on fresh resources.

The company has achieved zero liquid discharge at 16 of its 19 plants and plans to extend the system to the remaining facilities by 2030. It recycled 21.78 million cubic metres of water in FY26 and harvested 18 million cubic metres of rainwater.

Hindalco’s Mouda facility has also been certified as water neutral, with the company reporting no fresh water being sourced from outside for its operations there. Five mines have been assessed for water positivity, with water replenishment ranging from 1.5 to 16.6 times, according to Surawar.
Sustainability Linked To Accountability
For Hindalco, the sustainability push is also being built into its internal management structure.

Surawar said sustainability is not owned by a single department but is embedded across business governance, with key performance indicators linked to employee responsibilities from the board level to the shop floor. The company conducts monthly reviews of sustainability metrics, while dedicated sustainability and environment professionals work across its sites.

On emissions, Hindalco has achieved more than a 20 per cent reduction in specific greenhouse gas emissions and is expanding its renewable energy capacity. The company is also monitoring air quality across factories and townships, with initiatives covering particulate matter, sulphur oxides, cleaner transportation and dust control.
The approach extends to biodiversity, with 41 sites having biodiversity management plans and 6.26 million trees planted within the company’s operational areas.

Surawar said the broader objective is to make resource efficiency part of Hindalco’s manufacturing culture. The company’s sustainability strategy, she said, is ultimately about creating more value with fewer resources while maintaining long-term business growth.
Samiksha Choudhary
